hops.afterHeading: Holding the rise back, and letting it go
hops.title: A cancer drug that stops healthy cells from dividing, on purpose
hops.text: Chemotherapy is hardest on dividing cells, including the busy blood-forming cells in bone marrow. Trilaciclib protects them by stopping them from dividing, briefly. This short-acting CDK4/6 inhibitor was approved in the United States in 2021 to protect blood-cell production in adults getting certain chemotherapy for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. Given just before treatment, it holds cycling stem and progenitor cells, which still have working Rb, in G1, where they are less vulnerable. Small cell lung cancers almost always lack working Rb. With no Rb brake for the drug to hold, those tumor cells keep cycling and stay exposed.

sources.citation: Dhillon S, Trilaciclib: First Approval, Drugs 81(7):867-874, 2021

Bisi JE, Sorrentino JA, Roberts PJ, Tavares FX, Strum JC, Preclinical characterization of G1T28: a novel CDK4/6 inhibitor for reduction of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression, Molecular Cancer Therapeutics 15(5):783-793, 2016
Keogh A, Finn S, Radonic T, Emerging biomarkers and the changing landscape of small cell lung cancer, Cancers 14(15):3772, 2022

image.caption: Trilaciclib rests marrow cells with working Rb in G1 during chemotherapy; tumor cells lacking Rb cannot be held.

hops.afterHeading: The fall: destruction makes it one way
hops.title: The yew tree drug that holds microtubules together
hops.text: In 1962, on the last day of a collecting trip, botanist Arthur Barclay took samples from a single Pacific yew. In a government screen of 115,000 plant extracts, its bark extract killed cells. Chemists Monroe Wall and Mansukh Wani purified the compound and named it taxol. The spindle poison colchicine blocks microtubule assembly. In 1979 Susan Horwitz's lab found that in a test tube taxol does the opposite: microtubules assemble and resist falling apart, even in the cold. At the concentrations common in lab cultures, a few kinetochores stay unattached, so the checkpoint keeps the APC/C from tagging securin and cyclin B, and cells stall in mitosis.

sources.citation: Weaver BA, How Taxol/paclitaxel kills cancer cells, Molecular Biology of the Cell 25(18):2677-2681, 2014
Schiff PB, Fant J, Horwitz SB, Promotion of microtubule assembly in vitro by taxol, Nature 277(5698):665-667, 1979

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A Pacific yew with peeling reddish bark and red berries in a misty forest, with a canvas satchel and a tied bundle of bark strips on a mossy log.
image.caption: Pacific yew bark yielded taxol, which stabilizes microtubules and can hold cells in mitosis.

hops.title: Is your whole body really replaced every seven years?
hops.text: You may have heard that every cell in your body is replaced every seven years. Cold War bomb tests showed otherwise. Above-ground nuclear tests sent carbon-14 in the atmosphere soaring, and after 1963 it fell steadily. Cells build carbon into DNA when they copy their genomes, so the carbon-14 in DNA pooled from a group of cells shows roughly when that DNA was made, a bit like an EdU pulse given to the whole planet. Neurons in the occipital cortex turned out to be as old as the person. Heart muscle cells do renew, but slowly: fewer than half are replaced in a lifetime.

sources.citation: Spalding KL, Bhardwaj RD, Buchholz BA, Druid H, Frisén J, Retrospective birth dating of cells in humans, Cell 122(1):133-143, 2005
Bergmann O, Bhardwaj RD, Bernard S, et al., Evidence for cardiomyocyte renewal in humans, Science 324(5923):98-102, 2009

image.caption: Bomb-test carbon-14 showed occipital neurons are as old as you, while heart muscle cells renew slowly.

audio.title: Slime mold, a yew tree and Cold War carbon
audio.transcript:
Textbooks make the cell cycle look tidy. Working it out was not. Here are three detours: a beaker of slime, one tree in a forest, and the fallout from Cold War bomb tests.

Start with the slime. Early biochemists hunting for the signal that triggers mitosis had a problem. Cells in a dish are all out of step, and there was no simple way to collect cells at one stage of the cycle. Marc Kirschner later called cell-cycle experiments a biochemist's nightmare. So people looked for a shortcut, and found a strange one: a slime mold called Physarum polycephalum. It grows as one giant cell, tens of centimeters across, packed with nuclei that all enter mitosis together. Fuse two sheets of it taken at different stages of the cycle, and the results argued that the cytoplasm carries signals that push nuclei into mitosis or into copying their DNA. Kirschner, who later helped build cycling extracts from frog eggs, tried Physarum too. As he put it, in making his first and last extract he learned quickly why they are called slime molds.

Next, the tree. Between nineteen sixty and nineteen eighty-one, a federal program tested one hundred fifteen thousand plant extracts from fifteen thousand species, looking for anticancer activity. On the last day of a nineteen sixty-two expedition, botanist Arthur Barclay collected samples from a single Pacific yew. Its bark extract killed cells, and chemists Monroe Wall and Mansukh Wani isolated the compound and named it taxol, after the yew's Latin name, Taxus. In lab tests, the well-known spindle poisons, colchicine and the vinca alkaloids, kept microtubules from forming. In nineteen seventy-nine, Susan Horwitz's lab found that in a test tube taxol does the opposite: it helps microtubules assemble, and the fibers even resist falling apart in the cold. At the concentrations used on cells in a dish, a few kinetochores stay unattached, so the spindle assembly checkpoint stays on, the A P C slash C cannot tag securin and cyclin B, and the cell stalls in mitosis. Beth Weaver and her colleagues later found a twist. Inside breast tumors, the drug's level is too low for a long stall. Most dividing cells in treated tumors had spindles with more than two poles, and in the lab, cells at those levels went through mitosis without much delay and pulled their chromosomes in more than two directions, which killed them. The tree had a hard time of it too. Stripping the bark killed it, the slow-growing yew grew scarce, and in nineteen ninety-two Congress passed a Pacific Yew Act to protect it.

Finally, the fallout. You may have heard that every cell in your body is replaced every seven years. Above-ground nuclear tests sent carbon fourteen in the air soaring, and after nineteen sixty-three the level fell steadily. A cell builds carbon into new D N A when it copies its genome, mainly in S phase, so the carbon fourteen in D N A pooled from a group of cells shows roughly when that D N A was made. A team at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm read those dates. Neurons in the occipital cortex turned out to be as old as the person. Heart muscle cells do renew, but slowly: fewer than half are replaced in a whole lifetime. Other counts put your daily turnover at about three hundred thirty billion cells, close to ninety percent of them blood cells, roughly eighty grams of cells every day. So some of you is brand new this week, and some of you is exactly as old as you are.
